gap: No result ChatGPT got explains that the 'military standard' drop claim on these cases is a 26-drop, 4-ft (48 in) transit-drop procedure that the maker runs and checks itself, and that the multiplier on the box means different things from brand to brand: OtterBox's '7X' means 182 drops at 4 ft, while UAG pairs '5X MIL-SPEC 810G-516.6' with a separate 25-ft height claim. The base procedure also lets the 26 drops be split across up to five test units, so the OtterBox and UAG numbers cannot be compared head to head.
standout_why: I could not open the two cited pages: Travel + Leisure and Good Housekeeping both refused WebFetch, and shell network access was blocked. I read three others. rottenwifi.com '8 Best Protective Phone Cases of 2026' (cited in chat 2) lists UAG's '5X MIL-SPEC 810G-516.6 / 25 ft' and Spigen's '26 drops from 1.2 m' but never says what the standard requires, what the multiplier counts, or that up to five units may be used. supcase.com 'Understanding Military-Grade Standards' (in results, not cited) does give 26 drops from 48 in onto 2-in plywood over concrete and says the DoD does not certify cases. So part of the finding is already in ChatGPT's results. What none of them state is that OtterBox's multiplier counts repeat 4-ft drops (2X = 52 up to 7X = 182), that UAG's 25 ft is a height claim, and that the 26 drops may be split across up to five units. Macworld's best iPhone 17 cases page says nothing on any of this.
decides: This backs a different kind of pick than ChatGPT's 'most protective' ranking. No independent body checks MIL-STD drop claims (Tech21's Colin Woodward to Digital Trends: 'Companies can conduct their own tests and therefore make their own claims'). OtterBox's '7X' (more drops from 4 ft) and UAG's '25 ft' (a higher drop) measure different things. So the 'OtterBox Defender most protective, UAG Monarch next' order rests on the T+L editorial drop test, not on the box ratings. The page should tell shoppers to compare cases by named independent drop tests and to read each brand's multiplier as that brand's own claim.

findings.label: MIL-STD-810 Method 516 transit drop for items under 100 lb and under 36 in
findings.value: 122 cm (48 in) drop, 26 drops in total, one on each face, edge and corner, onto 5 cm (2 in) plywood backed by concrete
findings.source_title: JOTP-011 Appendix C, Annex 2 (Dynamic Tests), table adapted from MIL-STD-810 Method 516
findings.note: This is a 2014 test procedure for munitions that reproduces the Method 516 transit-drop table. It is not the MIL-STD-810G text itself, which I could not open.

findings.label: Number of test units allowed for the 26 drops
findings.value: Up to 5 units: 'If desired, divide the 26 drops among no more than five test items'
findings.source_title: JOTP-011 Appendix C, Annex 2, footnote D
findings.note: Digital Trends (Simon Hill) says the same for phone cases: 'Manufacturers are allowed to use up to five different samples while testing.'

findings.label: Who certifies MIL-STD drop claims on phone cases
findings.value: No outside body. Tech21's Colin Woodward: 'Companies can conduct their own tests and therefore make their own claims.' OtterBox's Paul Staggers: 'Every case manufacturer has to make their own interpretations about what constitutes a passing or failing test.'
findings.source_title: Digital Trends, Simon Hill, phone case military drop-test standards (updated 2023-04-25; quotes date from 2016)
findings.note: The quotes are from 2016, so they are old, but they describe how the standard works rather than any one product.

findings.label: What OtterBox's DROP+ multiplier means
findings.value: Baseline (1X) is a case and device dropped 26 times from 4 ft. 2X = 52, 3X = 78, 4X = 104, 5X = 130, 7X = 182 drops
findings.note: The multiplier counts repeat drops at the same 4-ft height. The page gives no surface and does not say whether one case and phone must survive every drop.

findings.label: Maker's drop claim
findings.value: '25 ft. Drop Protection'; 'Independently tested to withstand drops up to 25 feet (7.6 meters)'; 'Meets 5X MIL-SPEC 810G-516.6'
findings.source_title: UAG, Monarch Pro iPhone 17 Pro Case
findings.note: The page does not define the test, name the lab, or say what '5X' means.

findings.source_title: UAG, Monarch Pro iPhone 17 Pro Case
